This reigning world champion boxer is not a fighter

Jaismine Lamboria, 24, didn’t need aggression to punch her way to the top
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 6:07
Instaread

When I imagined a champion female boxer who is also an Indian army officer, I imagined someone stoic, who maybe gives one word answers and doesn’t crack a smile. But watching Jaismine Lamboria play the 2026 Commonwealth finals in Glasgow against Northern Ireland’s Michaela Walsh changed that. While Walsh appeared to have her jaw set in game mode, Lamboria was grinning right up to the minute the match began. It ended with her cinching her first Commonwealth gold.

To be fair, 24-year-old Lamboria has a lot to smile about. Hailing from Haryana’s Bhiwani district (also called ‘mini Cuba’ for giving India some of our best boxers, including Lamboria’s idol Vijendra Singh), she began training at 15, inspired by her uncles, the international boxers Sandeep and Parvinder Singh. Just 10 years later, she’s the reigning world champion in the women’s 57kg featherweight rankings, after winning gold at the 2025 World Boxing Championships (Liverpool). She became the first female boxer to join the Indian army, in 2022, right after she won bronze at her first Commonwealth Games. She’s also the first woman in her family to enter the ring.

However, when we met over a video call after weeks of co-ordination—she’s been deep in training for the upcoming World Cup Finals that will be held in Tashkent, Uzbekistan in November—I realised she’s just an easygoing person. I was greeted with a shyness that lasted exactly two minutes before she told me about her beginnings in boxing, carrying on her family’s legacy, meeting her idols and how she sometimes has to feign aggression to look the part.

Boxing champion Jaismine Lamboria’s winning mantra is keep calm and carry on punching

Tweak: At the Commonwealth finals, you were seen smiling right until the minute the match begins. How do you tap into the aggression you need the very next minute?

Jaismine Lamboria: To be very honest, I don’t know. I’ve never been naturally aggressive and what you see on my face [when the match starts] is not even aggression. I’m just focused on the right techniques. My coaches have to constantly ask me to be a bit more aggressive. I’ve just started working on this and even then it only comes because I want to improve myself.

T: You grew up watching your uncles’ boxing matches on TV with your family. Does your family follow the same tradition for your games now?

JL: Yes, absolutely. Whenever there’s a match that’s going to be televised, I already know all my immediate family, plus grandparents, cousins, uncles and aunts are going to be watching it—either together or if they’re travelling, then on their phones. I once video-called my parents after a match and I could see everyone had come over to watch my match together.

T: You used to play other sports in school and started boxing only as a teenager—what made you pick boxing?

JL: I didn’t play anything seriously, mainly just gully cricket with my friends. I always wanted to box, my uncles are both international level players and I wanted to be just like them. I actually told my mother about my interest in boxing when I was in the eighth standard. She said she would speak to my uncles but she probably thought it was just a one-off thing, so she didn’t tell them. But I kept asking her until she finally spoke to them a year later. My uncles and parents were supportive from the get-go, and my grandfather came around to it as well. So I officially began boxing training in the 10th standard.

T: Tell me about a punch you won’t forget.

JL: There are two actually, both from the same guy, from when I started out training with boys at my uncle’s academy in Budhwal. This boy was really good with left punches. So good I don’t remember the punches, because I had been completely knocked out. I have vague memories of my uncle helping me get home.

T: You’ve won so many matches in the last few years, are you a better boxer than your uncles now?

JL: [Laughs] No, I don’t think that’s possible. I think they will always be better than me at boxing.

T: You got a chance to train with [Olympic boxer] Mary Kom at the very start of your journey. What was that experience like?

JL: Mary Komji has been my idol since I started training—she and Vijendra Singh. I was still a new, entry-level boxer at the national academy [Netaji Subhas National Institute of Sports, Patiala], when I had that training session with her. I greeted her and didn’t even think she would speak to me, but she asked me how I was finding everything. And when we were training, she would come up to us and give us one-on-one suggestions like “Move this way,” or “You can hit better this way”. It was hard to keep a straight face through the session because I was so giddy on the inside.

T: What do you like to do in your free time, when you’re not training or working?

JL: I love to sleep, like a lot. And I like listening to music. Any genre, Hindi, Bollywood, Western pop and even Haryanvi. I will dance on my own in my room.

T: There are prejudices an aspiring female boxer might still face, like the idea that women are unsuitable for combat sports. What advice would you give to someone like that?

JL: I think for me, I was lucky to have a supportive family who didn’t think that I couldn’t play this sport. But if some people think women can’t be aggressive, well, we shouldn’t internalise it. We shouldn’t underestimate ourselves. I mean, I’m still learning how to be more aggressive but we shouldn’t ruin our game just because others don’t think we can do it.

Note: The interview was conducted in Hindi and has been translated to English.

This author did martial arts, ate platefuls of poha and drank gin with badass grannies across India

Jasreen Mayal Khanna’s new book will motivate you better than any self-help book

Ever been surprised by your own granny’s badassery? One minute you’re introducing her to a scandalous movie scene to see how she reacts, the next minute she’s telling you how she once punched a creep while walking to college in 1959?

In an ageist society like ours, it’s easy to relegate our grandmothers to the stereotypes of the sweet, servile custodian of traditional values. But if you show up with curiosity and attention, you’ll often find surprising stories of passionate, hardy women who pushed against norms.

This is how journalist and author Jasreen Mayal Khanna got the idea for her second book, Bullet Nani and Other Badass Indian Grandmas (Pan MacMillan). The book is inspired by her nani Pushpinder Kaur, who was eight months pregnant with Khanna’s mother when she left an abusive marriage. She went on to raise her daughter as a single mom, get her BEd degree, work as an English teacher.

After Kaur’s passing in 2021, Khanna spent a year thinking about the life her grandmother had managed to build for herself when women of that generation had all the odds stacked against them. She wondered if there were other grandmothers like hers, and set about looking for women of that generation who had been able to change the course of not just their own lives, but the lives of generations of their daughters to follow.

The book chronicles the stories of 12 such grannies from different corners of India, in whose lives you might find glimpses of your own nani/amammaa/baa/aaji/abok. There is the titular Bullet Nani Raminder Dhillon who faced off with the Taliban while on a UN mission in her 60s. And Thankam P., part of the first generation of female nuclear scientists, as well as Suman Dhamane, a tech-savvy content creator in her seventies better known as Aapli Aaji.

We spoke to Khanna about all the adventures she ventured on to speak to 100 grandmas across the country.

Tweak: You started research for this book with a simple Instagram story asking people about their grandma’s stories, but where did the idea originate?

Jasreen Mayal Khanna: I kept thinking about my grandmother’s life for an entire year after her passing. Then one day I ended up on a Reddit thread, where Indians were talking about all the wild things their grandmothers had done. All those stories had the same theme, of women standing up for themselves, and it was so similar to my nani’s journey. That was the germ of the idea—I realised that there might be more grandmothers out there, and it prompted me to put up the Instagram story.

T: What was the reaction to your story?

JMK: I had put up the story the evening before and the next morning when I woke up, I was like, what happened? Because the messages were pouring in. I had asked a few friends, influencers and NGOs to repost my story to help me get leads but I was not expecting it to go viral. That day I had to stay up till midnight, scribbling down all the names and handles because I was so worried that I would lose some of the leads. I put down almost 100 names on that Excel sheet.

T: How did you select the final 12 stories?

JMK: Initially I did calls with the kids and grandkids who had nominated their grandmas, because the women themselves would usually respond like, “What’s the big deal in what I did?” Many didn’t even identify as feminists. Once I got through those hundred names and knew I was writing a book, I hired my research assistant Priyam Moonka, and we started thinking of ways to find more grandmothers. We looked for women who might have already been featured in the news, if not national then local. Then we found Bullet Nani [Raminder Dhillon] through her TED Talk with Shah Rukh Khan. I knew that since these video shoots have time limits, there would be more to her story.

T: What were some of the challenges you had to face while working on the book?

JMK: I started writing this when my son was two, and the book was published after he turned six. And in between, I had to find a new publisher for the book as well. So I needed a lot of internal motivation to not abandon the project. And it was the grandmas that gave me that motivation, so whenever I got close to them, I would actually ask them, “How can I juggle all of this?,” and they would tell me I was on the right track, and I just needed to keep doing what I was doing.

T: Did you get to try any cool things while interviewing these cool grannies?

JMK: I’ve written about how Meenakshi amma [Meenakshi Raghavan, a grandma who has been practicing kalaripayattu since she was seven years old] made me pose with the weapons while I was there. I was giggling the entire time and she would keep telling me to stop smiling, “You have to look fierce!”. When I met Dr Rahmath Beegum [the first female doctor in the Lakshadweep islands], she fed me Lakshadweep-style biryani; the IPS officer Sridevi Goel offered me a gin and tonic and I gladly agreed, wanting to loosen up and have a frank chat. One of them even took me shopping and bought me a Kerala-style Kasavu saree. I’ve spent so much time with them, and that’s actually why I still feel close to them. I wish them on New Year’s, Diwali and on their birthdays.

T: Which story surprised you the most?

JMK: I think Pavane Mann’s story, of doing a round-the-world trip at the age of 54, and having a romantic fling on every continent. She made me question my ideas of what a grandmother should or should not do and I loved that. Why can’t a grandma have sexual revelation or learn to value her attractiveness? I asked her, “Did you never feel judged by everyone around you?” She said, “Everyone knew how I was, so they didn’t bother to bug me with judgement.”

T: Was there a common theme or trait you found in all these grandmothers’ stories, other than their candour or courage?

JMK: Resilience for sure. They were the OG hustlers. They had to become good at overcoming obstacles since there was no other way to live life on their own terms. And they did it with a lot of grace and patience—most of them weren’t even resentful if someone did them wrong. When I would do the interviews, getting them to dwell on the negative parts was hard. In fact, I felt like they had almost developed positivity as a coping mechanism.
